This is a use case: what a campaign gets, and in what order, when the brief is a press day.[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]The work is designed by a political cartoonist — chief designer for a Washington DC paper, and an editorial cartoonist before that. width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]A set of characters, built to be carried, plus the artwork they came from and the documentation from the day. • Four oversized heads — cane frame, papier-mâché skin, matte finish
• The character artwork — the same designs flat, for placards, posters and social
• A crate they pack into and travel in
• Stills and video from the day, cut for news desks and for vertical[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]The artwork is the part people underestimate. The heads are built from finished character designs, so the campaign also owns a set of drawings that work on a poster, a placard, a t-shirt and a social tile without redrawing anything. Where a brief calls for it, the same characters are animated as loops and projected after dark — see projection art and generative AI animation. The heads and the loops are designed together, so the projection is the same character.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="cartoonist" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="One frame, one argument" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Why a Cartoonist Designs This[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]A political cartoon and a protest photograph do the same job. Both get one frame to carry an argument, both are read in about a second, and both fail the same way — by needing explanation. Oddtoe drew editorial cartoons at college in Delaware, then worked as political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper. That is years of deciding which single image a political story runs with, and watching which ones an editor throws away. Not an abstract skill: it is knowing the reader gives you about a second, and building for that second.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]More recently, an illustration and cover design for a US House candidate’s fundraiser — a donkey bullying an elephant, which is exactly the kind of blunt, legible idea that survives being printed small. The same instinct decides what a protest object should be. Not the prettiest object, and not the biggest. The one a picture editor picks out of twelve on the wire. It also decides what to leave out. A head that needs a caption has already failed, and so has one that reads as a blob from across a square.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10" anchor="compare"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="Where the money actually goes" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Placards, a Stage, or Four Heads?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="2/3"][vc_column_text css=""]A campaign budget usually has one line for the visible part of an action. This is what that line buys three different ways.

 PlacardsA hired stageFour heads
What it costsCheap per unit, spent again every actionA large single-day hireOne build, amortised over years
How long it lastsOne rally, if it does not rainStruck by Monday morningYears, in a crate between actions
What a photo desk doesScrolls past itCrops it out of the frameRuns it, because nothing else looks like it
Who has to operate itWhoever is holding itA crew and a technicianFour volunteers
What you own afterwardsNothingNothingThe objects and the character artwork
[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="who" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="Campaigns, unions, and NGOs" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Who Commissions Work Like This?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]Non-profits and NGOs, grassroots campaigns, unions, advocacy organisations, and political campaigns. What they have in common is a date, a message, and a press list. Campaigns with a fixed date commission for a launch, a vote, or a summit, where one day has to produce a month of coverage. Unions commission objects that get used repeatedly, because the same members turn out several times a year.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]NGOs and advocacy organisations commission a visual identity that survives being used by volunteers in three cities without a designer present. Political campaigns commission artwork and objects the same way they commission any other asset. Oddtoe has done fundraiser illustration for a US House candidate. Agencies working for any of the above are welcome too: see experiential marketing.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="words" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="The bit that is not a service" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Why Oddtoe Makes Protest Work[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]Street art is punk rock for visual artists. You do not need a gallery, a commission or anyone’s permission, and the work is seen by people who did not choose to look at art that day. Few art forms can say that. Most of why this subject interests me sits right there. An object carried down a street is doing the same thing as a piece pasted on a wall at four in the morning: putting an argument where people actually are.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][vc_column_text css=""]I make my own work as well as client work, and sculpture street art is where I want to take that next. So a protest brief is not a category I added to a service list. It is the closest thing to what I would be making anyway. The practical upside for a campaign is that the person designing the object has a stake in whether it works. I want the photograph to be good for the same reason you do.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay=""][vc_column width="1/4"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/2"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="110" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="90" screen_tablet_spacer_size="70" screen_mobile_spacer_size="70"][vc_column_text item_animation="transition.fadeIn"]

Questions about

Protest work?

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_accordion style="style-3" active_section="1" font_size="18" tab_title_google_fonts="yes" tab_title_custom_fonts="font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal" icon_size="14"][vc_tta_section title="What is this use case, exactly?" tab_id="1757300000001-usecase-protest-faq-1"][vc_column_text css=""]

A worked example. It follows one brief - a campaign with a press day and no picture - from the first question through design, fabrication, the day itself, and what the campaign still owns afterwards. The same shape applies to any object-led action.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How long does it take?" tab_id="1757300000002-usecase-protest-faq-2"][vc_column_text css=""]

Six to eight weeks from brief to press day for a set of four heads. Design and approval take the first fortnight, fabrication the next three weeks, and the rest is packing and freight. A rush is possible but it comes out of the design stage, which is the part worth protecting.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Can they be shipped outside Australia?" tab_id="1757300000003-usecase-protest-faq-3"][vc_column_text css=""]

Yes. They are built to crate, and freight and paperwork are handled from this end. Cane and paper are plant material, so treatment and certification are part of the job rather than an afterthought.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What does a set cost?" tab_id="1757300000004-usecase-protest-faq-4"][vc_column_text css=""]

Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by how many characters, how large, how much structure each one needs, and where they have to travel. Send the brief and the date and you get a quote.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Do we need council permits?" tab_id="1757300000005-usecase-protest-faq-5"][vc_column_text css=""]

Usually not for the objects themselves - they are carried, not installed, with no power and no rigging. The permit conversation is about the assembly or the march, which the campaign is already having.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Can we use them more than once?" tab_id="1757300000006-usecase-protest-faq-6"][vc_column_text css=""]

That is the point. They go back in the crate and come out at the next action. A set built for one press day has usually paid for itself by its third outing.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Can you do the animation and projection as well?" tab_id="1757300000007-usecase-protest-faq-7"][vc_column_text css=""]

Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it - the same characters animated as loops and projected after dark. See projection art and generative AI animation.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Where is Oddtoe based?" tab_id="1757300000008-usecase-protest-faq-8"][vc_column_text css=""]

Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.

[vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_bg_style=”canvas” dfd_bg_image_canvas=”16244″ dfd_bg_image_repeat_canvas=”no-repeat” dfd_overlay_color=”#000000″ dfd_overlay_pattern=”transperant” dfd_overlay_pattern_opacity=”60″ dfd_row_config=”full_width_content” dfd_bg_color_value=”#161314″ anchor=”hero”][vc_column][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]

One press day, one photograph

Protest & Press Day

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark”][vc_column]

For non-profits, grassroots campaigns, and unions

Use Case: The Protest Press Day

[vc_column_text css=””]

Updated September 2026

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: what a campaign gets, and in what order, when the brief is a press day.[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]The work is designed by a political cartoonist — chief designer for a Washington DC paper, and an editorial cartoonist before that. It matters here because a rally photograph and a daily cartoon are the same problem: one frame, one argument, no second chance to explain.[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″ anchor=”the-day”][vc_column]
[vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″ anchor=”drawings”][vc_column]

Three studies, in progress

The Drawings Behind the Heads

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/6″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”2/3″][vc_column_text css=””]Three working studies, each answering a different question: how the thing is drawn, how people carry it, and how far the idea goes.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/6″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]
[vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”default_row_small_paddings” anchor=”what-you-get” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″][vc_column]

Objects, artwork, and the footage afterwards

What Does a Campaign Actually Get?

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]A set of characters, built to be carried, plus the artwork they came from and the documentation from the day.

• Four oversized heads — cane frame, papier-mâché skin, matte finish
• The character artwork — the same designs flat, for placards, posters and social
• A crate they pack into and travel in
• Stills and video from the day, cut for news desks and for vertical[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]The artwork is the part people underestimate. The heads are built from finished character designs, so the campaign also owns a set of drawings that work on a poster, a placard, a t-shirt and a social tile without redrawing anything.

Where a brief calls for it, the same characters are animated as loops and projected after dark — see projection art and generative AI animation. The heads and the loops are designed together, so the projection is the same character.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”default_row_small_paddings” anchor=”cartoonist” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″][vc_column]

One frame, one argument

Why a Cartoonist Designs This

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]A political cartoon and a protest photograph do the same job. Both get one frame to carry an argument, both are read in about a second, and both fail the same way — by needing explanation.

Oddtoe drew editorial cartoons at college in Delaware, then worked as political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper. That is years of deciding which single image a political story runs with, and watching which ones an editor throws away. Not an abstract skill: it is knowing the reader gives you about a second, and building for that second.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]More recently, an illustration and cover design for a US House candidate’s fundraiser — a donkey bullying an elephant, which is exactly the kind of blunt, legible idea that survives being printed small.

The same instinct decides what a protest object should be. Not the prettiest object, and not the biggest. The one a picture editor picks out of twelve on the wire.

It also decides what to leave out. A head that needs a caption has already failed, and so has one that reads as a blob from across a square.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″ anchor=”compare”][vc_column]

Where the money actually goes

Placards, a Stage, or Four Heads?

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/6″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”2/3″][vc_column_text css=””]A campaign budget usually has one line for the visible part of an action. This is what that line buys three different ways.

  Placards A hired stage Four heads
What it costs Cheap per unit, spent again every action A large single-day hire One build, amortised over years
How long it lasts One rally, if it does not rain Struck by Monday morning Years, in a crate between actions
What a photo desk does Scrolls past it Crops it out of the frame Runs it, because nothing else looks like it
Who has to operate it Whoever is holding it A crew and a technician Four volunteers
What you own afterwards Nothing Nothing The objects and the character artwork

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/6″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”default_row_small_paddings” anchor=”who” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″][vc_column]

Campaigns, unions, and NGOs

Who Commissions Work Like This?

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]Non-profits and NGOs, grassroots campaigns, unions, advocacy organisations, and political campaigns. What they have in common is a date, a message, and a press list.

Campaigns with a fixed date commission for a launch, a vote, or a summit, where one day has to produce a month of coverage.

Unions commission objects that get used repeatedly, because the same members turn out several times a year.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]NGOs and advocacy organisations commission a visual identity that survives being used by volunteers in three cities without a designer present.

Political campaigns commission artwork and objects the same way they commission any other asset. Oddtoe has done fundraiser illustration for a US House candidate.

Agencies working for any of the above are welcome too: see experiential marketing.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”default_row_small_paddings” anchor=”words” dfd_row_responsive_enable=”dfd-row-responsive-enable” responsive_styles=”padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10″][vc_column]

The bit that is not a service

Why Oddtoe Makes Protest Work

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]Street art is punk rock for visual artists. You do not need a gallery, a commission or anyone’s permission, and the work is seen by people who did not choose to look at art that day. Few art forms can say that.

Most of why this subject interests me sits right there. An object carried down a street is doing the same thing as a piece pasted on a wall at four in the morning: putting an argument where people actually are.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][vc_column_text css=””]I make my own work as well as client work, and sculpture street art is where I want to take that next. So a protest brief is not a category I added to a service list. It is the closest thing to what I would be making anyway.

The practical upside for a campaign is that the person designing the object has a stake in whether it works. I want the photograph to be good for the same reason you do.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=””][vc_column width=”1/4″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/2″]
[vc_column_text item_animation=”transition.fadeIn”]

Questions about

Protest work?

[/vc_column_text]

[dfd_accordion style=”style-3″ active_section=”1″ font_size=”18″ tab_title_google_fonts=”yes” tab_title_custom_fonts=”font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal” icon_size=”14″][vc_tta_section title=”What is this use case, exactly?” tab_id=”1757300000001-usecase-protest-faq-1″][vc_column_text css=””]

A worked example. It follows one brief – a campaign with a press day and no picture – from the first question through design, fabrication, the day itself, and what the campaign still owns afterwards. The same shape applies to any object-led action.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”How long does it take?” tab_id=”1757300000002-usecase-protest-faq-2″][vc_column_text css=””]

Six to eight weeks from brief to press day for a set of four heads. Design and approval take the first fortnight, fabrication the next three weeks, and the rest is packing and freight. A rush is possible but it comes out of the design stage, which is the part worth protecting.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Can they be shipped outside Australia?” tab_id=”1757300000003-usecase-protest-faq-3″][vc_column_text css=””]

Yes. They are built to crate, and freight and paperwork are handled from this end. Cane and paper are plant material, so treatment and certification are part of the job rather than an afterthought.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What does a set cost?” tab_id=”1757300000004-usecase-protest-faq-4″][vc_column_text css=””]

Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by how many characters, how large, how much structure each one needs, and where they have to travel. Send the brief and the date and you get a quote.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Do we need council permits?” tab_id=”1757300000005-usecase-protest-faq-5″][vc_column_text css=””]

Usually not for the objects themselves – they are carried, not installed, with no power and no rigging. The permit conversation is about the assembly or the march, which the campaign is already having.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Can we use them more than once?” tab_id=”1757300000006-usecase-protest-faq-6″][vc_column_text css=””]

That is the point. They go back in the crate and come out at the next action. A set built for one press day has usually paid for itself by its third outing.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Can you do the animation and projection as well?” tab_id=”1757300000007-usecase-protest-faq-7″][vc_column_text css=””]

Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it – the same characters animated as loops and projected after dark. See projection art and generative AI animation.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Where is Oddtoe based?” tab_id=”1757300000008-usecase-protest-faq-8″][vc_column_text css=””]

Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][/dfd_accordion][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]
